title: Duplicate loyalty point credits from non-idempotent earn events
text:
The events consumer that writes `earn` rows into `bronze.loyalty_transactions`
does not have an idempotency key. Each purchase event should produce exactly
one `earn` row per `order_id`, but the consumer's at-least-once delivery
guarantee means a redelivered message (consumer restart, brief downstream
timeout, rebalance) produces a second `earn` row with a new `transaction_id`
but the same `order_id` and `loyalty_id`. There was no uniqueness constraint
or dedup step to catch it — inserts were pure appends.

This is the same shape of failure Ibotta documented publicly: financial or
balance-affecting writes that aren't idempotent will eventually double-write,
because "redeliver on uncertainty" is the correct behavior for the messaging
layer and the correct behavior for the consumer is to make redelivery safe,
not to assume it won't happen.

title: Null loyalty_id join keys from an undetected upstream schema change
text:
The upstream event producer emitting purchase-earn events changed its
payload shape without a version bump or a heads-up to the loyalty-platform
team — a field rename in a client SDK release meant the field the consumer
mapped to `loyalty_id` stopped being populated for a subset of traffic (the
older SDK versions still using the old field name kept working; upgraded
clients silently sent null). The consumer had no schema validation on
inbound events — it mapped whatever fields were present and let anything
missing pass through as null, rather than rejecting the event or flagging
it.

This is the general shape of failure any pipeline hits once it has upstream
producers it doesn't control: a payload contract that isn't actively
enforced isn't really a contract, it's a suggestion, and it will eventually
drift without anyone downstream finding out until a join stops lining up.

title: Orphaned loyalty transactions from a late-arriving-dimension race
text:
`loyalty_accounts` and `loyalty_transactions` are populated by two
separate write paths — account creation happens on enrollment, transaction
writes happen on purchase — and there is no ordering guarantee between
them. A customer who enrolls and makes a purchase in the same session can
have their purchase-earn event processed by the transactions consumer
*before* the enrollment consumer finishes committing the new account row,
if the account-creation path is even slightly slower (a retry, a brief
downstream lock, ordinary queueing delay under load). The transaction
lands referencing a `loyalty_id` that is valid and will exist momentarily,
but doesn't exist yet at the instant the transaction consumer commits.

This is the classic late-arriving-dimension problem: a fact row can
legitimately arrive before its dimension row when the two are written by
independent, unsynchronized processes, and any pipeline that assumes
dimension-before-fact ordering without enforcing it will eventually see
this class of race.

text:
1. Quantified the problem: `left join` from `loyalty_transactions` to

   of the audit (the account had since landed, just after the transaction),

   join failure was transient at read time only if queried in the race

   existence before committing a transaction row; if the account isn't
   found, the event is retried with backoff for a bounded window (covering
   ordinary write-path latency) before quarantining, rather than writing
   an orphaned reference immediately.

title: Negative point balances from a redemption race condition
text:
The redemption path read `points_balance`, checked it against the
requested redemption amount, and wrote the decremented balance back — three
separate steps with no locking or atomic compare-and-set between them. Two
redemption requests for the same account arriving close together could
both read the same (sufficient) balance, both pass the check independently,
and both write a decrement — the second write landing after the first,
based on a balance that was already stale. Neither request was wrong in
isolation; the bug is that "read balance, check, write" isn't a single
atomic operation, so two concurrent instances of it can both succeed when
only one should have.

under normal load and only shows up when a customer (or a script, or a
retried client request) fires two redemptions close enough together to
land in the same race window.

should have a matching row in `bronze.loyalty_accounts`.

```sql

from bronze.loyalty_transactions t
left join bronze.loyalty_accounts a on t.loyalty_id = a.loyalty_id
where a.loyalty_id is null
  and t.loyalty_id is not null
  and t.transaction_timestamp >= now() - interval '24 hours';

doesn't automatically mean "confirmed orphan."

text:

that produces transient false positives would halt otherwise-healthy loads
over races that fix themselves. Contrast with RULE-001, where every
violation is a real, permanent duplicate with financial exposure attached —
there's no "wait and it resolves itself" case there.

text:
This does not block ingestion. Rationale: an inactive gold account is a
cost leak (subsidized perks going to a customer who's stopped engaging),
not a financial-ledger error the way a negative balance or a duplicate

load pipeline over stale tier assignments would be disproportionate to the
actual risk; the right response is flagging the accounts for the
reassessment job to correct, not stopping ingestion until it's fixed.

already (mis)moved.

title: Gold-tier activity-recency check
text:
Before PM-005, the nightly tier-reassessment job's health was monitored by
process exit code only — "did it complete without error" — not by whether
it actually touched the accounts it was supposed to reassess. A schema
change upstream caused the job's core query to silently match zero rows;
the job kept reporting success while doing nothing, for an unmeasured
period before an unrelated account-health audit noticed the tier
distribution didn't match activity recency. This rule exists to catch the
*symptom* (stale gold accounts accumulating) independently of whether the
reassessment job itself is healthy, so a future silent job failure is
caught by this check even if the job's own monitoring is fooled again the
same way.
